listing.shortDescription: Decode JWTs, check expiry and verify HMAC signatures in your browser.

title: JWT Decoder: Decode JSON Web Tokens Locally
description: Decode a JSON Web Token's header and payload in your browser, see iat, nbf and exp as dates, check expiry, and verify HS256/384/512 signatures locally.
quickAnswer: A JWT is three Base64URL-encoded parts separated by dots: a header, a payload of claims, and a signature. Decoding the first two parts shows their JSON, but it does not prove the token is genuine; only checking the signature with the right key does. This decoder runs entirely in your browser and can verify HS256, HS384 and HS512 signatures with a secret you type.

formula.title: How a JWT Is Decoded and Verified
formula.expression: JWT = Base64URL(header) . Base64URL(payload) . Base64URL(signature)   ·   HS256 signature = HMAC-SHA256(secret, header + '.' + payload)
formula.explanation: Each part uses Base64URL encoding (RFC 4648), which swaps + and / for - and _ and drops = padding. Decoding the header and payload gives UTF-8 JSON. The time claims iat (issued at), nbf (not before) and exp (expires) are NumericDate values: seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, shown here as UTC and local dates. For HMAC algorithms, the signature is recomputed over the exact header and payload text with the secret, using the browser's Web Crypto API, and compared in constant time. Tokens signed with RS256, ES256 or other public-key algorithms need the issuer's public key and are not verified here.

variables.description: The claims: who the token is about (sub), who issued it (iss), the audience (aud), times and any custom data.

variables.name: Signature
variables.description: Proof that the header and payload were created by someone holding the key and were not changed.

commonMistakes.title: Trusting a decoded token
commonMistakes.description: Anyone can create a token with any payload. Decoding only reads it. Your server must verify the signature with the correct key and algorithm, and check exp, nbf, iss and aud, before trusting any claim.

commonMistakes.title: Putting secrets in the payload
commonMistakes.description: A signed JWT is encoded, not encrypted: anyone who has the token can read the payload. Never put passwords, card numbers or other secrets in it.

commonMistakes.title: Accepting alg: none or switching algorithms
commonMistakes.description: Libraries must only accept the algorithms you expect. Allowing 'none', or letting an attacker switch from RS256 to HS256, are classic JWT vulnerabilities listed by OWASP.

commonMistakes.title: Pasting production tokens into websites
commonMistakes.description: A valid token is a password for as long as it lasts. Only paste tokens into tools that run locally, like this one, and prefer expired or test tokens.

commonMistakes.title: Using a weak HMAC secret
commonMistakes.description: HS256 secrets such as 'secret' can be guessed offline from any token. Use a long random key, at least 256 bits for HS256, as RFC 7518 requires.

faqs.q: How do I decode a JWT?
faqs.a: Paste the token into the box. The header and payload are Base64URL-decoded and shown as formatted JSON, with time claims converted to dates.

faqs.q: Is it safe to paste my JWT here?
faqs.a: Decoding and signature checks run in your browser. The token and secret are not sent anywhere, stored, logged or added to the page address. Even so, avoid pasting live production tokens into any website you do not control.

faqs.q: Does decoding a JWT verify it?
faqs.a: No. Decoding only reads the contents. A token is trustworthy only after its signature has been verified with the right key, and its expiry and audience have been checked.

faqs.q: How do I check if a JWT is expired?
faqs.a: Look at the exp claim: it is a Unix timestamp in seconds. If it is earlier than the current time, the token has expired. The decoder shows exp as a date and marks expired tokens.

faqs.q: How do I verify an HS256 JWT signature?
faqs.a: Enter the shared secret in the signature section and press Verify. The HMAC is recomputed locally with Web Crypto. For the jwt.io example token the secret is your-256-bit-secret.

faqs.q: Can I verify RS256 or ES256 tokens here?
faqs.a: Not at the moment. Those use public-key signatures and need the issuer's public key (often from a JWKS URL). Verify them in your application with a maintained JWT library.

faqs.q: What is the difference between JWT, JWS and JWE?
faqs.a: A JWT is a set of claims. When signed it is a JWS (three parts) and its payload is readable; when encrypted it is a JWE (five parts) and the payload can only be read with the decryption key.

faqs.q: What do iat, nbf and exp mean?
faqs.a: iat is when the token was issued, nbf is the earliest time it may be used, and exp is when it expires. All three are seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC.

common-jwt-claims.heading: Common JWT Claims
common-jwt-claims.td3: Who created and signed the token
common-jwt-claims.td6: Who the token is about, often a user ID
common-jwt-claims.td9: Which service the token is meant for
common-jwt-claims.td12: After this time the token must be rejected
common-jwt-claims.td15: Before this time the token must be rejected
common-jwt-claims.td21: A unique ID, used to stop a token being replayed

decoding-is-not-verifying.heading: Decoding Is Not Verifying
decoding-is-not-verifying.p1: The header and payload of a signed JWT are only encoded, so they can be read by anyone and changed by anyone. What stops tampering is the signature: if a single character of the header or payload changes, the signature no longer matches. A server must therefore:
decoding-is-not-verifying.li1: Verify the signature with the expected key and an allow-list of algorithms, never the algorithm named in the token alone.
decoding-is-not-verifying.li2: Check the times: reject tokens past exp or before nbf, allowing only a small clock skew.
decoding-is-not-verifying.li3: Check who it is for: iss and aud must match your issuer and service.
decoding-is-not-verifying.li4: Keep tokens short-lived and send them only over HTTPS, as RFC 8725 recommends.
decoding-is-not-verifying.p2: This page is for reading and debugging tokens. HMAC signatures are checked with the browser's Web Crypto API, and the token and secret are kept only in memory while the page is open. For generating random secrets, see the password generator; for hashing text, the hash generator.

errors.tooLong: That token is too long to decode here.
errors.whitespace: A JWT cannot contain spaces or line breaks. Copy the token again without them.
errors.jwe: This looks like an encrypted JWT (JWE, five parts). Its payload cannot be read without the decryption key.
errors.partCount: A JWT has three parts separated by dots (header.payload.signature), but this one has {{count}}.

header.notBase64Url: The header is not valid Base64URL.
header.notUtf8: The header is not valid UTF-8 text.
header.notObject: The header must be a JSON object.
header.notJson: The header is not valid JSON.

payload.notBase64Url: The payload is not valid Base64URL.
payload.notUtf8: The payload is not valid UTF-8 text.
payload.notObject: The payload must be a JSON object.
payload.notJson: The payload is not valid JSON.

errors.signatureNotBase64Url: The signature is not valid Base64URL.
errors.noWebCrypto: Signature checks need the Web Crypto API, which this browser does not provide.
errors.unsupportedAlgorithm: This token uses {{alg}}. Only HS256, HS384 and HS512 (shared-secret) signatures can be checked here.
errors.noSecret: Enter the secret to check the signature.
errors.secretNotBase64: The secret is not valid Base64 / Base64URL.
errors.noSignature: The token has no signature to check.

status.noExp: No expiry (exp) claim: this token does not expire by itself

verify.unsigned: This token is unsigned (alg "none" or an empty signature). It proves nothing about who created it.
verify.hmac: This token uses {{alg}}, an HMAC signature with a shared secret. Type the secret to check it here, in your browser.
verify.other: This token uses {{alg}}. Only HS256, HS384 and HS512 can be checked here; public-key algorithms such as RS256 need the issuer's public key in your application.
verify.failed: The signature could not be checked.
verify.valid: ✓ Signature valid: this {{alg}} token was signed with this secret.
verify.invalid: ✗ Signature invalid: the token was not signed with this secret, or it has been changed.
